partycohesion: PartyCohesion card. Headline: Do members of Congress vote the same way no matter who is president? Beside it, a half-circle chart of every House member as one dot, colored by party and ordered by voting record. Source: Voteview.
same-bill-different-vote: Card titled Same bill, different vote. Large number: 3,718 times a member voted for a bill at one stage and against it at another while most of their party voted the same way both times. Bar chart by Congress, labeled by starting year: 2007: 491, 2009: 903, 2011: 550, 2013: 464, 2015: 313, 2017: 260, 2019: 304, 2021: 157, 2023: 189, 2025: 87. The last bar is a Congress still in session.
respect-for-marriage-act: Card about the Respect for Marriage Act, H.R. 8404. Headline: 9 House Republicans voted differently in December than in July 2022. Two boxes: 47 Republicans voted Yea on passage in July, and 39 on the final version in December. Yea, then Nay: Cliff Bentz (OR), Mario Diaz-Balart (FL), Brian Mast (FL), Dan Meuser (PA), Scott Perry (PA), Maria Salazar (FL), Jefferson Van Drew (NJ). Nay, then Yea: Michael Gallagher (WI), Jaime Herrera Beutler (WA).
senate-unity: Line chart titled In the Senate, party unity moves with the White House. Two lines, Senate Democrats and Senate Republicans, showing average party unity per Congress from 2007 to 2025. Democrats go from 91.6% to 95.3%, Republicans from 85.3% to 98.6%. At each of the last three changes of president (2017, 2021, 2025), senators from the new president's party voted with their party more often than in the Congress before, and the other party's senators less often.
congress-final: Card titled The 118th Congress, final record. Four boxes with average party unity: House Democrats 96.7%, down 1.8 points from the 117th; House Republicans 93.0%, down 1.6 points from the 117th; Senate Democrats 98.3%, down 0.7 points from the 117th; Senate Republicans 90.5%, up 2.9 points from the 117th.
floor-remarks: Card titled Said it on the floor, then voted that way. Two grids of dots, one per member who took a clear position in floor debate on Ukraine aid or the Respect for Marriage Act. Filled dots voted the way they spoke: 101 of 101 House members and 44 of 47 senators.
